newsitem.title: FRANCE: U.S STUDY SEES LOWER NATO EXPANSION COSTS.
newsitem.headline: U.S STUDY SEES LOWER NATO EXPANSION COSTS.

text.p: A new U.S. study estimates that NATO expansion will cost America an extra $150 million to $200 million a year, considerably less than earlier projections, U.S. officials say.

The projections are based on assumptions that the alliance will not permanently deploy troops in its new east European member states and that the military threat from Russia at present is virtually nonexistent, they said.
These are among details now emerging which Washington hopes will soothe Russian concerns and boost NATO's case for expanding into former Warsaw Pact countries.
In addition, while U.S. officials say they remain opposed to giving Russia a veto over NATO decisions, the alliance has offered Moscow something of a compromise on cooperation.
An alliance vow of more intense formal consultations with Russia in a joint consultative council is already well known.
But U.S. officials said that on a case-by-case basis, the alliance also could envision joint decisions between NATO and Russia on certain initiatives outside NATO's boundaries.
That would essentially give Moscow, in these particular cases only, a veto over how the initiatives were carried out.

These cases would not be spelled out in the NATO-Russia charter. But one official said a Nagorno-Karabakh peacekeeping effort or plans to jointly deploy a theatre missile early warning system could be examples of this kind of joint action.
However, if Russia opposed an initiative at the outset, NATO still could proceed if it chose to, the official said.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on a whirlwind world tour aimed in part at building support for NATO's position on enlargement, is expected to discuss these and other details when she meets Russian leaders in Moscow on Thursday and Friday.
She meets NATO foreign ministers in Brussels on Tuesday.
Russia opposes alliance expansion and has been dragging its feet in negotiations on a proposed charter defining a special new relationship with NATO in the post-Cold War era.
Moscow says NATO membership for former Warsaw Pact states will threaten Russia's security, give ammunition to President Boris Yeltsin's political foes and create divisions in Europe.
Albright has insisted that viewing NATO as a military threat is "old think" and she is determined to persuade Moscow that NATO is keen on genuine cooperation as part of a united Europe.

The study on enlargement costs has several purposes including proving that NATO expansion is affordable and that the allies have thought through the consequences of extending security guarantees to new members, senior U.S. officials said.
Also, it would underscore U.S. and allied assurances that an expanded NATO is not a threat to Russia, officials said.

A controversial study by the Rand Corp last year estimated that alliance expansion likely would cost $30 billion to $52 billion over a 10-15 year period. This put the extra U.S. liability at upwards of $700 million annually.

U.S. officials expect some complaints they are deliberately "low-balling" the costs to win domestic support. But senior officials said a major assumption of the new study was that the threat facing NATO now is far less than what RAND predicted.

"The RAND study assumed a continued steady level of threat (that NATO would have to be prepared for) while the study coming out this week assumes virtually no threat" from Russia, one official told Reuters.
U.S. official say that, even if Russia turned away from democracy and once again made threatening moves toward the West, it would take Moscow eight to 12 years to build up its forces.
The study, which was ordered by Congress and carried out by the Pentagon with State Department assistance, is expected to be made public later this week. REUTER
